disposition: same trial protocol and different route
assessment: APOLLO used intranasal peanut oil as the matched comparator in postviral smell loss. The protocol has inconsistent no-treatment wording, and no oral arm or Parkinson population.

The protocol discusses psychological effects and hazards of smell loss. The two intranasal arms were designed for olfactory outcomes and related quality of life, without a separate fall-frequency, depression or anxiety endpoint.
The experiment tested isolated S-carvone in memory and locomotion assays. Spearmint appears as a source of carvone enantiomers. The nociception and CNS depressant remarks refer to other experiments.
The experiment used isolated S-carvone and mentions apathy in a general description of brain disorders. It supplies no clinical apathy outcome or caraway arm.

disposition: species discrepancy between protocol and results
assessment: The published arm is called peppermint and reports epigastric pain among gastrointestinal outcomes. The registry calls the arm spearmint oil. Spearmint also appears in the published bibliography. The plant identity of the administered arm needs reconciliation.
Constipation appears in tuberculosis background and cited work. Ginger was administered, and the reported symptom panel in Figure 4 does not include constipation.
Ground ginger and placebo were compared during tuberculosis treatment. Figure 4 tracks epigastric pain as part of a gastrointestinal panel. No Parkinson cohort or general pain estimate is reported.
Olive oil was used in an alternate printed gel. The investigators measured antioxidant properties and texture in the laboratory with no participant swallowing outcome.
Corn oil carried quercetin in a rat arthritis arm. The study gives no corn-oil-only arm or reported pain severity comparison. No rat met the rescue analgesia threshold.

The arthritis study tested oral pumpkin seed oil nanoemulsion with and without quercetin. Paw swelling and composite arthritis severity were reported. The daily pain assessment governed rescue analgesia and does not provide a pain outcome estimate.
Oral walnut oil was studied in rat spatial-memory tasks. Pain and anxiety occur in background or references on acid-sensing ion channels. Neither symptom was evaluated after oil feeding.

Salmon, cod liver oil and soybean oil are named as dietary fatty-acid sources in the introduction. The randomized arms received krill and macadamia oils. No separate outcome after eating the named ingredients was estimated.

A cited experiment used sardine-derived oil and measured working-memory physiology in healthy older adults. RRIPP-3 measured anxiety and fatigue in a separate krill-versus-macadamia comparison without a sardine arm.
Macadamia oil was the oral comparator. State anxiety showed no clear treatment effect against krill oil in military officers. No oil-free arm or Parkinson group was included.
Piperine and black pepper oil appear in cited dysphagia studies. This rat experiment used isolated allyl isothiocyanate on laryngopharyngeal tissue.

Topical allyl isothiocyanate triggered rat swallowing reflexes. The compound occurs in mustard, wasabi and horseradish. The experiment did not test culinary ground mustard or Parkinson swallowing difficulty.
A cited study used nigella oil for metabolic endpoints in diabetic dialysis. Fatigue occurs in the background of the almond oil constipation trial. Nigella was absent from its arms.
The bibliography names a separate extra-virgin olive oil abdominal massage trial. The current trial used almond oil and does not evaluate olive oil for constipation or anxiety.
Ginger and olive oil appear in cited oxidative-stress or inflammation work. This obesity study gave cold-pressed avocado oil and found no clear group difference in plus-maze outcomes.
Cold-pressed avocado oil had no clear plus-maze effect in obese mice. The experiment did not use refined oil or a Parkinson model and gives no clinical anxiety estimate.
